content:
Who is the department that decided Wang Fuk Court residents cannot return?

During the Q&A session, multiple owners raised the issue. At least five questioners challenged Hop On, asking which government department made the decision to bar residents from returning to Wang Fuk Court and what was the legal basis for the lockdown. Hop On failed to give a direct answer on the first four occasions, merely saying that Wang Fuk Court has not yet been unsealed, that it is beyond the manager's authority to make arrangements, and advising owners to contact their dedicated social worker if needed — provoking an outcry from owners in several venues.

Hop On does not know on what legal basis the authorities imposed the lockdown

Solicitor Leung Ping-chiu eventually responded that Hop On did not know on what legal basis the authorities imposed the lockdown, but it would be inappropriate for Hop On to explain on their behalf lest it misinterpret the government's considerations. As for the survey reports on the other seven blocks of Wang Fuk Court, which also attracted much attention, Hop On said the typhoon and rainy seasons were approaching and the findings might be released once the authorities completed their surveys. Hop On also said that after taking legal advice, it considered the request to fall outside Hop On's responsibilities as manager.

Owners concerned government using donations to reclaim titles — can it save compensation by not rebuilding?

The government had earlier said it would not rebuild on the original site. At the meeting, several owners questioned whether this meant the HK$2 billion "fire insurance" payout, calculated on the cost of restoring the building's structure, would not be honoured. "If the government uses donations to take back the titles and doesn't rebuild, does that save China Pacific compensation?" A China Pacific Insurance (Hong Kong) representative surnamed Lau said that once policy liability was established, the company would pay out in accordance with the policy terms regardless of whether repairs or rebuilding were undertaken, and that the acquisition would not affect policy liability or the calculation of the amount. However, Lau also said that specific policy and legal liability matters could only be further assessed after the independent committee and relevant government departments had completed their investigations and published the findings.

Repair costs for Wang Chi House estimated at HK$30 million

Hop On also reported on the situation at Wang Chi House, which was unaffected by the fire. Hop On had earlier said that repairing Wang Chi House would cost at least HK$30 million and take at least nine months, involving re-tiling of external walls and restoration of electrical systems. Today, Hop On updated the total to around HK$32 million and the works period to between three and nine months. Solicitor Leung Ping-chiu, invited by Hop On to attend the meeting, pointed out that under the deed of mutual covenant, Wang Chi House formed part of the entire estate, and separating it out would require the consent of all owners and substantial amendments to the deed — a complicated and costly procedure.

Some owners noted that Hop On had cited the time needed to contact owners as a reason for not convening an owners' meeting within the statutory deadline, yet had successfully issued subsidy cheques on behalf of the Urban Renewal Authority earlier this year. They questioned: "I want to ask, what's so difficult? You can't find us owners to hold a meeting?" Eric Chan, Hop On's Property Services Director who chaired the meeting, did not give a direct answer, saying it was a venue issue — that finding a venue capable of accommodating a thousand people was very difficult, and the meeting could only proceed after the Home Affairs Department provided a venue. An owner criticised the explanation as unreasonable: "Hong Kong has so many mega events, easily putting on shows with tens of thousands in one venue, and you tell me you can't find a venue for our 2,000 people? That's really hard to accept — I hope you won't use this as an excuse again."

"It's not at all what we wanted"

Ms Kwan, speaking to the media again as she left early, said the owners' meeting had failed to address her questions. "The ball just gets kicked around — this is not at all what we wanted." China Pacific had said the insurance payout depended on the independent committee's report and the findings of the relevant departments. Ms Kwan believed the acquisition deadline of 31 August made waiting pointless: "All the answers will only come after 31 August. By then, if we've sold, nothing will concern us anymore." She had submitted an expression of intent but had not yet signed a sale and purchase agreement. After attending the owners' meeting, she felt they should first "insist on not selling" and only sell after 31 August once there were answers. "Otherwise, if you sign everything before 31 August, all the reports will come out afterwards — we won't even be owners, so what has it got to do with us?"

As for the next owners' meeting, Ms Kwan said if it were scheduled in two months' time and she had chosen to sign, she would no longer be an owner and would have no right to attend. Asked why the next owners' meeting seemed to be set for two months later, she retorted: "Then you help me ask (Hop On) why two months later? Why does the (independent committee) only release its report in October?"

Wang Tai House resident Kitty shared the view that the owners' meeting could not answer her questions. The issue most people cared about, she said, was insurance compensation: "The insurance assessment won't come out until September sometime (note: China Pacific said it depended on the independent committee's report and the relevant departments' findings) — September. By then we've already sold in August, so even if the report comes out, the insurance won't concern us!" She also criticised that the next owners' meeting might not be held for another two months: "Two months later, I've already sold my flat — what's the point of holding a meeting?" Regarding Hop On's response on whether owners could attend meetings after selling, Kitty called it "playing tai chi": "They basically said it: once you've sold, it's none of your business." She also worried the government might legislate to acquire owners' titles: "If I don't sell my title to you, do I have to go to jail? If you solve my problem, then of course I'll sell to you." Kitty hoped to find a place she liked, criticising the resettlement units as much smaller in floor area than Wang Fuk Court. "They're not big enough to live in. And if I want a bigger one, the compensation won't be enough to buy one!" She made clear she would not sign a sale and purchase agreement for now: "It's already been said — once you sign, nothing concerns you, you don't even have a share when we go back upstairs. We hope for a third time going back upstairs."

Mr Chan, who in the morning had accused Hop On of being a government puppet, said he already knew everything he needed to know beforehand: "After asking many questions, they just went round in circles — they couldn't answer." For example, he had asked whether, in the absence of a rebuilding or repair plan, the HK$2 billion in compensation for the building's damage by natural disaster needed to be paid out. "The insurance company was just wandering around the garden, acting as if it couldn't read Chinese — they didn't answer, they answered irrelevantly, nothing to do with the question." Mr Chan was also concerned about the legal aspects of claiming compensation. He noted that Hop On's explanation of legal procedures was that "it might be a very lengthy process, needing a team of lawyers — and if we sued and lost, we owners might have to share the legal fees."

He described Hop On's slides as portraying things negatively, and when he pushed back, he said lawyers or legal representatives should do their utmost to protect their clients' interests. Before initiating litigation, they should give clients an estimate of the chances of success, and if successful, apply to the court for the other side to pay legal costs. "The lawyer confirmed this, but it was only because we asked that they mentioned it. The more positive points only came out after we asked." Mr Chan believed owners were dissatisfied with the meeting arrangements, starting with splitting everyone into different venues. "I don't believe Hong Kong has nowhere that can accommodate 2,000 flats — with two representatives per household, that's 4,000 people. A concert at Kai Tak holds 50,000!" He said even the Hong Kong Stadium would be fine; air conditioning wasn't essential.

Mr Chan also said that owners had received calls or authorised representative details the day before, and accused Hop On of "moving the goalposts" when it at one point restricted attendance to just one representative per flat. He believed the various venues had all been highly contentious: "Under our pressure — or rather, when we kicked up a big enough storm — they backed down. But they were obstructing us. I always say Hop On should be helping us, not hindering us." Asked whether he thought Hop On had helped them, he replied: "Helping us? What have they helped us with? I don't see how they've helped us at all." As for the date of the next owners' meeting, Mr Chan said bluntly: "Anyone with a normal mind wouldn't expect it to be held before 31 August." He explained that some residents had requested a meeting in the week before 31 August, but Hop On again cited venue difficulties, saying it would be very hard to arrange. He therefore had no expectations. He said he had not yet signed a sale and purchase agreement and would "see how things go" then, describing the current situation as like a blind-box lucky draw — nothing was guaranteed, and there was little incentive to sell the unit.
